name: Thinkers and Tinkers: The Pioneers of Computing
description: From a mathematician's mechanical dreams to wartime machines and the founders of the personal computer: the people who built computing, and their machines.

checkpoints.name: Dreams of engines
checkpoints.note: Leibniz imagined calculating machines, Babbage designed the Difference Engine and then the Analytical Engine, and Ada Lovelace saw that it could do more than arithmetic. Punched cards, first used on looms, became a way to feed data to machines, and Boole's algebra of logic would later underpin digital circuits.

checkpoints.name: War and the first programs
checkpoints.note: Zuse's relay machines, Colossus at Bletchley Park, the Harvard Mark I and ENIAC arose under wartime pressure. Turing described what any computer can do, and Manchester and EDSAC ran stored programs.

checkpoints.name: Big machines, new languages
checkpoints.note: UNIVAC sold computers to business, Backus led Fortran, Hopper pushed toward COBOL, and McCarthy's LISP shaped AI. Hamilton wrote the software that helped land Apollo, run on its small guidance computer.

checkpoints.name: Unix and the personal computer
checkpoints.note: Thompson and Ritchie made Unix and the C language, the Xerox Alto showed a screen driven by a mouse, the Altair 8800 sparked the hobbyist market, Wozniak and Jobs built the Apple, Gates wrote software for it all, and Kahn and Cerf designed the shared protocols for ARPANET and the internet.

checkpoints.name: The web and open source
checkpoints.note: Berners-Lee gave the internet a web. Torvalds released Linux for anyone to use and improve, and van Rossum created Python, which became popular with beginners and scientists.
